en: The *Bhaktiśataka*,
composed by the great scholar Rāmacandrabhāratī:
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Awakened One!
He whose knowledge encompasses all things, whose word is irreproachable, in whom not even a trace of passion exists— much less hatred or delusion—
and whose causeless compassion is boundlessly sweet, bestowing happiness upon infinite sentient beings.
Whether he be the Buddha or Giriśa, we pay homage to that Blessed One. || 1 ||

Lord Śambhu is not your enemy, nor is Hari; he is neither your adversary, nor indifferent, nor your kinsman. Furthermore, the Self-born One (Brahmā), nor others such as Indra and the rest, nor even the Buddhas, are your teacher, your friend, or your father in this world, for you share neither the same lineage nor the same birth.
But among these, he who is free from passion and all-knowing is the one to be served by the wise. || 2 ||
Brahmā is overcome by ignorance and embraced by the great illusion so difficult to master;
Viṣṇu, out of excessive passion, holds Pārvatī upon his own body;
whereas that Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, is free from ignorance, free from illusion, and devoid of passion in this world.
"Tell me, tell me, O brothers: who among them should be served by the wise for the sake of liberation?"
Having attained in many ways the states of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśvara through various causes, alas, they wander again in saṃsāra, that abode of absolute suffering.
Of what use are those states for embodied beings, which abound in misfortune and possess a beginning and an end?
Therefore, one should always aspire for the state of Buddhahood, which is without beginning, middle, or end. || 4 ||
The form of consciousness— subtle, all-pervading, pure, devoid of shape, effortless, formless, the seed of limitless compassion,
undecaying, the knower of all, free from all limiting adjuncts, and the bestower of immortality through its sovereignty.
May that object, which is to be resorted to by those who have conquered the bodiless god of love, become my refuge. || 5 ||
Subtler than the subtle, unimpeded by afflictions, infinite, and greater than the great; having conquered the world through his majesty, possessing abundant compassion;
two-armed yet armless, two-footed yet footless, and bestowing gifts even upon the three [enemies].
Having two eyes yet being eyeless, possessing qualities yet being devoid of qualities—that indeed is my refuge.

Ever-blissful, the truth, the heart of aesthetic essence, the abode of eloquent speech, worthy of service by the virtuous, having perfectly realized reality, with an equanimous mind, self-established, the goal to be attained, the bestower of all fruits, and possessing a gentle countenance.
May that reality, which is my own and belongs to all, be my refuge. || 7 ||

This [work] concerns the Self-Existent One who possesses direct knowledge, who removes the fear of existence, who is free from dread, whose fortune radiates, who has abandoned worldly enjoyments, who possesses great heroism, and who has conquered passion;
it is fourfold in its paths, pure in nature, and likewise devoid of an agent.
May that Reality, which is the most excellent in the world, extend its vast joy throughout all realms of existence.
In some places blue, in others yellow, and in some places red;
in some places with the luster of the moon, and in others beautiful with the hue of madder; in some places possessing a brilliant radiance—thus it proceeds from the intermingling of colors.
Bearing six crests upon those various things, that reality is my refuge. || 9 ||
Invincible, with a complexion as radiant as Jāmbūnada gold, the triple refuge, the triple vehicle, the triple wisdom, the protector of the three worlds, and the triple speech;
a vessel of compassion, with a gentle smile, wearing a beautiful saffron-colored robe.
I take refuge in the one who has performed meditation, whose feet are fixed in the siddhāsana posture. || 10 ||
With a pair of eyes like blooming blue lotuses, he repeatedly expounds the Tripitaka out of compassion for the multitudes of gods and men;
supremely peaceful, he regards gold, stones, silver, and clods of earth with equal equanimity.
May that object be my refuge, providing a novel hospitality for my eyes. || 11 ||
"I go for refuge to the Buddha, the most excellent of beings; I follow the Dharma, the foremost of those free from passion;
I go for refuge to the Saṅgha, the preeminent among assemblies."
Furthermore, I go for refuge three or two times. || 12 ||
Once again I go for refuge to the Buddha; once again I make the Teacher of the World my teacher.
Once again I speak, I praise, and I pay homage.
O Gautama, my satisfaction with you is not at all complete. || 13 ||
Having repeatedly surveyed the three worlds, I have taken refuge in the pollen of the lotus of your feet; this is my sole shelter and my only deity.
I have no other refuge; there is none, there is none, there is none. || 14 ||
Homage again and again to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, who proclaim that "all is impermanent, suffering, and non-self. 15.
O Lord free from passion, I bow to your very feet; O Indra among Sages, I thus revere you again and again,
repeatedly, beyond and even further beyond.
I bow to those above, on both sides, in the cardinal directions, and in the intermediate directions. || 16 ||
O Lord of Sages, you have traveled by whatever path, and you have stood, sat, or even lain down in whatever place through the power of yoga.
I bow even a hundred times to that meritorious sacred ford.
In whom the Blessed One himself was born, in whom all was awakened, where the Wheel of Dharma was turned, and where it was most clearly illuminated— where...
I bow even to that which filled the nectar of immortality. || 18 ||

To him who is the royal swan in the lotus-pond of the wheel of omniscience, whose splendor is as beautiful as the kunda flower, the moon, and the jasmine; who is worshipped by the hosts of gods; who is co-emergent with the wheel of the true Dharma; and who is the celestial *pārijāta* tree for all beings.
I bow with devotion to the stainless, glorious Tooth Relic. || 19 ||
Above the abode of the Nāgas, upon the summit of the circular range of the earth, on the peak of the golden mountain situated at Trikūṭa,
stands the image of the inexhaustible relic placed at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Bearing upon my head with reverence the foremost shrine of the Jina. || 20 ||
Having attained him— who possesses a jeweled trench within his golden basin and whose root is the awakening of the Lord of Mountains, radiant upon the diamond throne—
the Buddha immediately thereafter achieved victory over Māra.
I bow down to that Blessed One, who possesses omniscience. || 21 ||
O head, bow to the Buddha; O ear, always listen to the Dharma spoken by the one who teaches non-duality;
O eye, behold everywhere the incomparable form; O nose, smell the lotus feet;
O tongue, praise the Friend of the Sun (the Buddha); and O friend, you should worship the Cloud of Glory (Śrīghana).
O mind, contemplate this: the abode of the Jina at Vraja’s feet is perfected and possesses our own virtues. 22.

The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—this triad is a great, priceless jewel. O seeker of liberation, from this day forward, I entrust my very self to these three, which destroy the fear of the three realms of existence. From now on, I shall be devoted to them; there is no other supreme refuge for me—this is the truth.
May I become his disciple; I bow down a hundred million times to this one praised by the thirty gods. || 23 ||
O Sage, I do not seek gain or honor, nor am I terrified by fear, nor do I desire fame; it is not because you are born of the lineage of Dharmāṃśu, nor out of a desire for knowledge,
nor have I approached you for refuge through tradition, but rather because of your universal benevolence.
Having discerned right knowledge, I have set out to cross the ocean of existence through you. || 24 ||
Having fallen into the ocean of sandalwood paste— the radiance of your various virtues such as dispassion, compassion for all beings, and wisdom— no one else is capable of leading you away,
whether it be kings who punish you, gods who revile you, or even your own kinsmen.
O Jina, my father, I cannot live even for a moment without you. 25.
Whether my dwelling be in heaven, in hell, among the animals, or in the city of the asuras, or perhaps in the city of the pretas, or anywhere else by the force of karma—
O Omniscient One, from there to there, may I hear Your virtues that flow like nectar to the ears.
My mind takes refuge in those who are free from sin; I have no other prayer for happiness. (26)
I am indeed your servant, captured by you through the price of my virtues;
I am indeed your disciple, disciplined by you through your own words.
I am indeed your son, having attained that state and finding happiness through the recollection of you.
O Guru, O Buddha-Svāmin, O my father, protect me from existence! 27.
You are father, mother, brother, and sister; you are the steadfast friend and kinsman in times of calamity, the sovereign, and the supreme preceptor for the initiation into immortality.
You are sovereignty, you are enjoyment, you are wealth and grain, and you are majesty.
O Omniscient One, you are my fame, my knowledge, and my very life—everything for me. 28.
O Sage among Sages, free from passion, ocean of compassion,
Sugata who has shattered the vast cage of cyclic existence,
Buddha who has attained the nectar [of liberation], [open] the lotus of my mind.
O sinless one, let this be my perfumed chamber for you.
In this wheel of saṃsāra— which is selfless, impermanent, impure, consisting of suffering within suffering, and without end—
you alone are the Lord capable of protecting me; O Ocean of Compassion!
O Lord, therefore be gracious, be gracious, be gracious! || 30 ||

Be gracious, O Lord, Lord of Gods, Lord of the World, Victorious One, Adored by the Universe, Adored by me, Adored by the Virtuous, Buddha! O Non-Terrible One, Enemy of Existence, Enemy of Smara, Enemy of Darkness!
I am yours alone, devoted to you with body, speech, and mind.
He is your son of noble family; he alone is your devotee; he becomes the bearer of the burden of your teaching; he is your disciple; he has come for refuge; and he alone is your servant.
Whoever should not transgress your command by any means whatsoever. || 32 ||
O Buddha! Benefiting the world alone is your worship; harming it, O Lord of the World, is your affliction.
O Victor! How am I not ashamed to harm the world?
I declare myself a devotee of your lotus feet. || 33 ||
Wealth, people, power, your own body, and the kingdom— all these you have bestowed a hundredfold for his benefit; yet this world belongs to that harmful wrongdoer who seeks to injure you.
Where are my compassion, sympathetic joy, and loving-kindness? || 34 ||
Like an unfaithful wife, the movement of the mind departs from you, leaving behind the five objects of desire;
moreover, for one who pursues sense-objects, the attainment of liberation is impossible.
O Lord of Sages, what indeed shall I do? Grant me your service.
O most beloved one, Supreme Person, Foremost Buddha, remover of weariness, Siddha, whose fame is renowned throughout the world;
be my refuge, O you who possess unsurpassed grace!
Day by day, I am indeed the slave of your slave. || 36 ||
O Ten-Powered One, I am weak in this age of strife, submerged in the high surging waves of the ocean of long-standing misdeeds;
how may I follow Your ship of Dharma?
O Jina, grant me the support of your compassionate hand. || 37 ||
Having observed the manifold suffering of existence and being terrified by fear, I have prostrated myself before you many times;
O Supporter, [save me] as I fall through exceedingly heavy craving.
O Jina, grant me the support of your compassionate hand. || 38 ||
O Jina, your compassion for the world is indeed impartial; therefore, out of your grace, may I, who am defiled by faults,
become free from pride and happy.
The ear, as it were, moves through both the good and the bad with equal attention. || 39 ||
Blinded by the mass of accumulated and abundant delusion,
devoid of compassion, bereft of the scent of self and kin,
stripped of virtue and knowledge, and risen with sin.
O Friend of the Wretched, quickly [remove] the lack of discernment in people. || 40 ||
Whatever heavy misdeeds I have previously committed with my body, speech, and mind,
may they all dissolve away moment by moment.
O Omniscient One, by the remembrance of Your feet.
O Sugata, O you of sweet intelligence, I have fallen prostrate upon the earth before you with a full-length prostration;
by your power, may all my unwholesome deeds be purified.
Let it fall down; let it not rise up again, [falling] together with it. || 42 ||
I worship only your lotus-feet;
I honor only your lotus-feet;
I meditate upon only your pair of feet.
Your very feet are my eternal deity. || 43 ||
I speak of no one, I do not worship anyone, I do not praise anyone, I do not think of anyone, nor do I feel affection for anyone; having abandoned all, I take refuge in no one.
I am your servant; I am your footman. || 44 ||
In every assembly, in every word, on every path, in every house, and in every dwelling here,
my mind is established, awakened, and filled with water upon every piece of earth.
One should indeed constantly meditate upon this Lord of the World. || 45 ||
I behold the Buddha incessantly with a mind free from passion, as if with my very eyes;
for I sleep at night having placed you within my heart.
The separation from you is not equal for me; they alone [are so]. 46.
Indeed, for me here today, a cloudy day would be a foul day;
yet a day shrouded by dark clouds is not a foul day for me,
since it bears the name of the jewel-like Buddha, who is like nectar.
May that day not be one devoid of mindfulness for him. || 47 ||
O Giver of Immortality, Possessor of the Six Super-knowledges, King of Dharma,
Honored by the Three Worlds, Lord of Sages, Gautama— those men who recite [this name] day after day...
I bow to those blessed ones who are honored by the Rāhus. || 48 ||
"O Daśabala, Jina, Siddha, Vajrabuddhi, Sugata, Tathāgata, Buddha, Śākyasiṃha!"— whoever utters this at any time or in any place, [attains success].
I bow even to him, though he be born of a lineage of slaves. || 49 ||
O Conqueror of Madana, O Teacher of those who have been defeated, O Lord of Wealth, O Leader, O Most Excellent among the All-Knowing,
O Best of Poets, O Sovereign of Speakers, O Pure One—
O Śākyamuni, O Sage, you who are rich in generosity, be gracious! || 50 ||
O Lord of Men, even after drinking the nectar of immortality,
they once again suckle at the teat of a bitch;
yet one who has tasted even once the essence of the nectar of your speech—
He never again enters the womb of a mother. || 51 ||
O Blessed One, I am not able here to endure the affliction of birth, old age, death, and the like.
Have mercy on me; I do not know the directions, and having considered that, I behold the suffering of animals and other such beings.
Reflecting further upon that, my mind trembles helplessly at the thought of being rendered powerless over my hands, feet, eyes, and other faculties in old age.
O Jina, O Lord, what can I do? Be gracious! || 53 ||

I direct my thirst toward that object which produces happiness, even though it has never been seen before and has only entered the path of hearing; for this very reason, I do so incessantly toward the seed of peace.
My mind turns toward you and finds delight in you alone. || 54 ||
Therefore, my mind does not find delight in the happiness of gods and men enjoyed in succession,
even though it is experienced day after day like sugar-candy.
For even one who has seen the faults [of such conduct] practices abstinence. || 55 ||
A fool disregards, by his very gestures, an invaluable wish-fulfilling gem held in the palm of his hand;
how then could I abandon the Jewel of the Buddha?
In this world, he is wealthy, virtuous, and wise.
He is wise, he is of noble birth, he is virtuous, he is famous, and he is a hero;
he alone is honored in the world and truly happy.
O Jina, he who possesses unwavering devotion toward you— || 57 ||
Indeed, by him everything has been studied here;
indeed, by him everything heard has been put into practice;
indeed, the entire universe has been conquered by that unconquered one.
O Jina, he whose devotion toward you is perfectly steadfast. || 58 ||
Out of respect for his own tradition, a person does not look upon another's doctrine; even though it takes away his life, he does not abandon it out of reverence for his mother.
Indeed, a child should not release a poisonous potion into his ear. || 59 ||
"I am the best of poets, O Jina; you are my scholar. How could I abandon you, who have been so well-grasped?
For you dispel the continuous stream of unwholesome tendencies that have arisen."
The excellent vision is accompanied by the rays of the sun. || 60 ||
For a person who has turned his back on the state of the Sugata, what is the use of asceticism, what is the use of fame, and what is the use of anything else?
For a person who has turned his back on the state of the Sugata...
What need is there for austerity or fame, and what need for anything else? || 61 ||
May those who have no devotion for the feet of the Sugata never even be born upon this earth;
such has been declared here regarding men who have committed transgressions.
The destiny of hell is certain, and not otherwise.
O Jina, [I see] a king who has mastered all the sciences,
born of a noble lineage, possessed of excellent form, youth, and other qualities,
yet who does not worship you.
Let the mind cast off its impurity like a low-born person by birth.
One who has abandoned intoxication, pride, and envy;
who possesses compassion, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration; who is discerning;
and whose devotion to your feet is firm—even such a person, though born of the lowest caste—[is liberated].
May that best of men be my friend in every successive birth. || 64 ||
For a devotee who has performed the worship of the feet of the Jina,
even a life of ten days is praiseworthy;
but not [a life] of a thousand million times a hundred thousand kalpas.
Of one who has performed the worship of the lotus feet of the Lord of Munis. || 65 ||
He becomes a companion to the celestial beauties and joyfully accepts worship offered by others with devotion;
O Teacher of gods and men, [this is the fruit of] your worship—
If, due to some incapacity, one should be unable to perform it in that manner. || 66 ||
Even that noble person who, in this world, brings your image— so beautiful, exceedingly variegated, and of wondrous form— within the range of his vision, is abandoned by [worldly existence].
O Lord of Poets, [this] evil deed accumulated over a very long time—67.
He who bows before an image of those two fashioned from jewels, gold, stone, and so forth,
obtains here a fruit equal [to that of bowing before the actual beings] through the clarity of his mind.
O Conqueror, he who bows before you, which is superior even to the restraint of anger, [attains the highest state]. || 68 ||
The wise person who performs even a single act of worship at your lotus feet with forest flowers becomes one whose crown is adorned by the garlands from the heads of the hosts of gods bowing down.
One resorts to that which is blazing and stainless; therefore, it is sovereignty. || 69 ||

O holy Samantabhadra, refuge of the multitude! If there should arise even a single moment of thought that is identical in form to the vast mass of merit born from taking refuge [in you], then [all] the entire...
Then that [state] surpasses even the sky. || 70 ||
O Sage, those who are delighted by the recounting of your virtues enter into those very virtues of yours;
just as when the moon rises, its clear light enters the moonstone.
That frost-like mass of rays was like a handful of grain. || 71 ||
O Lord, Sugata, even once something was offered by a person who had abandoned delight in worldly existence;
that [offering], O Sugata, cuts through all [defilements] with its blade—
You have spoken of the faults such as the influxes (āśrava) like a tree. || 72 ||
Whatever good deed is performed here with a false view indeed results in its own bitter ripening;
just as the essence of earth and water [yields] its own bitter state.
It leads [the mind] just as a sown seed of the picumarda tree [grows]. || 73 ||
Having fallen at your lotus-like feet, one never again falls into the four miserable realms;
for a person who performs wholesome deeds never [falls].
O Protector, no one at all goes to an evil rebirth anywhere.
Having understood this through your instruction,
I am devoted to the worship of your lotus feet;
may the Blessed One confirm this for me in age after age.
Casting aside evil intellect, may there be noble devotion in birth after birth. || 75 ||
O Blessed One, even though it is steady for a moment at your word, the host of enemies— hands, feet, eyes, and so forth—
forcibly agitates the heart.
O Lord without a protector, O Masterless One, protect this, protect this! || 76 ||
If he strives to bring the eye under control, then the ear flows away;
following that, the tongue, the nose, and the body—
Alas! In this way, they are mutually difficult to grasp. || 77 ||
The course of the exceedingly fickle mind in this world shall be unobstructed like that of the wind in the sky; yet,
by some means, it gradually attains steadfastness.
This [world] is overcome through practice and through detachment. || 78 ||
Although my mind is naturally clear, it may have been rendered dark by the long-accumulated stains of sin;
how indeed might it be washed clean by the drops of the water of virtue?
By means of those [merits] acquired by me with such a mind, [may this be so]. || 79 ||

O supreme among men, [save] me, whose stream of consciousness has been rendered turbid by passion, and who am intensely tormented by mental anguish, with the flowing streams of the nectar of your most pure words.
Purify me instantly; I bow down like a staff. || 80 ||
O Sage, the teacher of all, when you are pleased, what is difficult to attain here or what is difficult to attain there? For those whose minds are pure, they are the servants of you.
They do not respect even the status of the Lord of the Gods, even in their minds. || 81 ||
The senses produce fear in abundance when grasping at objects as if they were poison, due to the perception of their defects;
for one who has well understood the defect of the future burning [of passion] does not [act thus].
Even a child might grasp the tip of a lamp flame. || 82 ||
O Victor, as long as this [body] has not yet grown old through indulgence in the demons of the sense-objects,
one should immediately apply it to virtuous deeds.
I have come to you, who are affectionate toward those who have sought refuge in you. || 83 ||
Even this— sons, wife, my own body, home, and so forth— if I know it to be like the water of a mirage,
then both "mineness" (*mamatā*) and "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*) veil me.
For even that is a most serious manifestation of delusion. || 84 ||
Everything is born from its own cause,
and it is discarded, decays, and perishes by its own cause;
for I too am likewise a mere heap of elements.
"How am I his? And how, O Sage, is this mine? (85)
In this world, for one in whom the notion of a self arises, that notion produces egoism;
that [egoism] further expands the craving for worldly existence.
That very [ignorance] repeatedly generates delusion. || 86 ||
By means of that [ego-sense], one performs actions, both auspicious and inauspicious; for those indeed produce suffering within the three realms of existence.
Therefore, the notion of a self is the very root of suffering.
O Jina, cut that down with the sword of my words. || 87 ||
Then [he saw] the knower of all, the ocean of compassion, the cause of the causes of the three worlds, the noble one,
who has gone everywhere, the infinite, the existence of peace—
I praise the Lord, the swan in the minds of the sages. || 88 ||
O Lord, during bathing, ritual acts, eating, giving, smelling,
and likewise listening; during meditation, touching, seeing, and so forth, as well as in conversation and the like—
in the morning, evening, by day, and by night— [my mind remains] in Your lotus feet.
O Lord of Sages, may my mind always take delight in you, as the hearts of young men do in a young woman. (89)

O my Master, O wish-fulfilling tree for my desires, O my Deity, O my Guru, O my Mother, O my object of worship, O my dear friend, O my true refuge, O my Father, O my Knowledge, O pacifier of all my remaining sufferings, O my Contemplation, O my Abode!
O one liberated by me, O you of my noble fortune, O destroyer of my distress, O awakened one for me—protect me! || 90 ||
O Sugata, in praising you, Brahmā became downcast; the Guru lost his gravity; the Sun, the leader of the day, became leaderless;
Viṣṇu fell into thirst; the poet ceased to be a poet; and even Īśvara became powerless. Śeṣa, whose power is that of the serpent-king, had his speech as Indra shattered in your praise.
O Lord of gods and men, who am I—a deluded and wretched being—to praise your virtues?
The body of that meritorious one, upon which the marks of a Great Man shine brilliantly with the eighty secondary characteristics— ten times two plus twenty—
does not even equal a sixteenth part [of his splendor].
Even the host of gods, headed by the four-faced Brahmā, [is thus]; what then to say of men? || 92 ||
Like the fresh rainbow of Mahendra upon the Golden Mountain, a beautiful halo of radiant light constantly shines everywhere;
for whomever it comes within the range of their vision here, let them hasten.
It removes that unsurpassed darkness from within and without to a great distance. || 93 ||
Your form is captivating to the eyes; your speech bestows a flood of bliss upon the ears; your compassionate influence utterly deludes the world; and your tranquility is supreme.
O Blessed One, your scholarship is renowned throughout the worlds by the very name "Omniscient."
And the renunciation of sovereignty in the prime of youth is clearly the ultimate limit of dispassion. || 94 ||
The gods have recognized your heroism in the face of adversaries through the crushing of their pride;
for by your arrows, this world—including its gods and asuras—was conquered with ease.
Your realization of nirvāṇa has most clearly manifested your valor.
What can we say of the power and majesty of the Blessed One, by which this world was made difficult to bear? || 95 ||
Since you even condemn in the Veda the ritual for slaughtering goats and horses, you are compassionate toward living beings; therefore, there is no one greater than you in mercy.
Thus, these perfections of your virtues are not within the scope of the intellect of those whose nature is envy.
Those fools prattle on, "Alas! This Sugata is one who reviles my doctrine. || 96 ||

May that Fortune of your excellent fame— which is the companion of the foam on the Mandākinī as it gently stirs against the breasts of the celestial beauties plunging therein, and which is the friend of the white water-lilies of the Ocean of Milk—
not fail to embrace me now, even though I am so unfortunate.
O Blessed One, physician for attachment, disease, and the like—this too is my prayer. || 97 ||
Those virtuous ones who go for refuge to you, O Buddha, do not go to an evil rebirth;
having abandoned their human bodies, they then obtain divine ones of unsurpassed bliss.
[They are freed from] bad dreams, ill omens, wicked serpents, malevolent planets, and evil beings.
Even painful and severe diseases do not, in certain cases here, approach those who are virtuous in this way. || 98 ||
Brahmā held a spotless parasol made of jewels for him; Cakrapāṇi [Viṣṇu] held a chowrie;
the bards were Hara, Guru, and the Serpent; Mahendra was the conch-blower;
and others, bowing with devotion, had lamps, water-pots, banners, and flowers shining in their hands.
O Lord of Sages, they remained there expounding the Dharma for you as you descended from heaven to the earth.
He who regards the wife of another as his own mother, who has no longing for the wealth of others, who does not speak falsely, who drinks no intoxicants, who does not kill living beings,
who fears the violation of moral boundaries, whose heart is compassionate, and who has abandoned all pride— [such a man is truly noble].
O Blessed One, he alone, being righteous in soul, is capable of performing the worship of your feet.
In this world, he who has desisted from all killing of living beings, from seizing the wealth of others, from sexual union with women, from false speech, and from intoxicants;
and from eating at improper times, from the dalliance of songs, garlands, perfumes, and ornaments, and from high beds and seats— [he attains the highest state].
O Teacher of gods and men, that very wise one was thirsty; he is indeed your son—of this there is no doubt. (101)
The paths of stream-entry and so forth, endowed with the six factors, destroy the defects of passion and the like;
those defects, their roots severed and their existence-destinies destroyed, attain peace along with their fruits.
For the nine paths, the abandonment of afflictions is the cause of the eternal, deathless, and undecaying state.
The cause of these phenomena is your word, O Jina; the cause of that [word] is you alone. 102.
Having shattered the twenty mountains of the view of a self-identity with the vajra of stainless wisdom,
they uproot all karma arising from the end of evil passions such as attachment and aversion;
thus, there are four who have attained the path, and likewise four who possess the corresponding fruits.
Therefore, O Lord of Munis, we do not consider the Noble Saṅgha to be separate from you. (103)
Just as space is infinite, so too are all sentient beings infinite; this entire vast expanse of the world-system is infinite.
Having realized this through your infinite course of wisdom, O Jina, you speak thus.
And you alone, O Buddha, know your own infinite virtues in this way. || 104 ||
May devotion toward the Blessed One— the infallible destroyer of worldly existence— persist in birth after birth;
may righteousness always be my instructor in every way.
Let it be, let it be; the Saṅgha is the unsurpassed field of merit. || 105 ||
By whatever pure and abundant merit has been earned here through praising you, the Buddha, who are worthy of honor in the three worlds,
may all sentient beings in the world [attain] the enlightenment of a Perfectly Awakened One by means of that.
May they, having shaken off various evils through meditative cultivations, proceed [to liberation]. || 106 ||
While the illustrious Parākramabāhu, the lord of Laṅkā, the supreme sovereign of kings, the sun to the lotus-clan of the radiant Bhaṇus, was ruling the earth with statesmanship,
there lived the wise Śrī Rāmacandra, a true Gauḍa and a divine priest (Bhāratikṣitisura) among poets.
He composed the *Bhaktiśataka*, known by the name *Śrītṛṇa*, which bestows dharma, artha, and mokṣa. || 107 ||

The *Bhaktiśataka*, composed by the great scholar, the master Bhūsurendra— a supreme lay devotee of the Blessed One, the Lord Śākyamuni, the Omniscient, and a sovereign of the glorious Buddhist scriptures from the land of Gauḍa— is hereby completed.
The king, whose arms were endowed with valor, the crest-jewel among rulers of the earth,
and the friend of the circle of scholars, made that Rāmacandra— the twice-born who was the ocean of poetry— a sovereign of the Buddhist scriptures.

May the Buddha, the Victorious One, be victorious for me; may the teaching of that Blessed One remain stainless; may it shine for the benefit of sentient beings; and may the Saṅgha, its support, likewise flourish. May the kings, headed by the Lord of Laṅkā, always protect the earth with diligence.
May the clouds rain at the proper time, and may all living beings attain loving-kindness. || 2 ||

The disciple of the venerable Śrī Rāhulasvāmin— the lord of sages, the preeminent teacher of the royal lineage, whose eloquent speech belongs to the Lord of the Three Piṭakas, the ascetic who is the master of the village of Tīrtha—
is the wise Sumaṅgala Muni; [this work] is composed by him in his own language.
Out of compassion, he has narrated this commentary on the *Munīndrabhaktiśataka*. || 3 ||
Homage to the Buddha, the Teacher; homage to the Dharma, the instruction;
homage to the great Saṅgha—constant homage to all three. (4)
Success!
